news.2026-10-16-ethiopie-erythree-ruptur: Adigrat, Tigray (northern Ethiopia), near the Eritrean border
Eritrea cuts ties with Ethiopia, which keeps saying it wants access to the Red Sea
After Ethiopia expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats, Asmara cut relations. Addis Ababa says Eritrean soldiers entered Tigray; Eritrea denies it.

Ethiopia told the UN Security Council that Eritrean soldiers had advanced up to 60 kilometres inside Tigray, its northern region. Eritrea denies this and sees it as a pretext for war. Reuters could not independently verify the incursion [1][2].
Ethiopian forces and their allies returned to Adigrat, about 30 kilometres from the border, after Eritrean troops pulled back. According to ACLED, Ethiopia used drones against them [2].
Eritrea announced it was cutting diplomatic relations after Ethiopia expelled 10 of its diplomats and closed its embassy in Asmara [1][2].

A country of more than a hundred million people with no coastline risks falling out with the neighbour that has ports. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed keeps repeating that Ethiopia must reach the Red Sea; he says he wants it through peace and dialogue, but Eritrea accuses him of preparing a war of aggression [2].

The two countries reconciled in 2018 and reopened their border crossings, then relations deteriorated again. Fighting has also resumed between the Ethiopian army and an opposition alliance that includes the TPLF, which weakens the November 2022 peace agreement [2].
You are not directly affected, but the Red Sea is a route for world trade. A new conflict in the Horn of Africa adds one more risk in an already tense region.

news.2026-10-16-namibie-boeuf-europe-fie: Europe shuts its door to Namibian beef because of foot-and-mouth disease
Since 6 October, the European Union has suspended part of its meat imports from Namibia, after an outbreak in the south of the country.

A European regulation adopted on 2 October came into force on 6 October: it suspends imports of fresh beef, sheep and goat meat, some farmed or wild hoofed animals, and products such as biltong [1][3].
Foot-and-mouth disease was confirmed on a commercial farm in the Karasburg district; the outbreak was declared on 22 September and affected 11 farms [1][2].

There are exceptions: meat that has undergone the EU's strictest risk-reduction treatment can enter, and fresh meat certified before 23 September can still arrive for 90 days. Namibia's preferential access to the European market is unchanged [3].
The European Union is by far the main customer for Namibian beef: more than 80% of its beef exports [1].

The sector was already fragile: beef exports fell 41.1% between 2024 and 2025, from 22.7 million to 13.4 million kilos, according to the Namibia Meat Board [1]. European buyers are already turning to other suppliers [2].
If you buy imported meat, other countries may take Namibia's place on the shelves. For Namibian farmers, it is an immediate loss of income.

news.2026-10-16-afghanistan-route-wakhan: Wakhan Corridor, from Broghil to the Chinese border (Afghanistan)
The Taliban open a road to China so they no longer depend on Pakistan
A 121-kilometre road now links the Wakhan Corridor, in north-eastern Afghanistan, to the Chinese border. It is not yet a real commercial crossing.
The Taliban government inaugurated on 4 October a 121-kilometre road running from Broghil, opposite Pakistan's Chitral district, to the “zero point” of the Chinese border [1][2].
It cost about 365 million afghanis, close to 5.5 million dollars, and was built by Afghan engineers without foreign advisers [1]. According to a Pakistani commentator, it is not paved [2].
According to Asia Times, opening the road does not mean a commercial crossing is already working [1].

Until now, Afghanistan, which is landlocked, has depended on Pakistan for its goods: they pass through Karachi and the Torkham and Chaman crossings [2]. This road gives a way to China that avoids Pakistani territory [1][2].

The context matters: Afghanistan complains about Pakistani air strikes, which Pakistan says target militants, and China worries about armed groups near Xinjiang [1]. For Beijing, it is also a way to depend less on Pakistan and the CPEC corridor [1].
This has no direct effect on your shopping, but it is a clear example: when a country is cornered, it builds a road elsewhere to change its dependencies.

news.2026-10-16-venezuela-fmi-pas-de-dol: Venezuela says no to the dollar and presents its oil and mining plan to the IMF
On 14 October in Bangkok, the economy vice-president promised more oil and minerals to repair water and electricity, and ruled out dollarisation.

Economy Vice-President Calixto Ortega presented on 14 October, at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, a plan to raise oil and mineral output and reinvest the revenue in water and electricity, neglected for about a decade [3].

He ruled out adopting the US dollar as the country's currency: the bolívar should eventually serve the whole domestic economy. The central bank speaks of a “progressive remonetisation” of the bolívar and aims for an inflation target in the medium term [1][2][3].
The IMF says it is discussing a technical office in the country, but Venezuela has not requested a financing programme [3].
Venezuela is trying to reopen its door to world finance. The IMF forecasts growth of 5% in 2026 and 7% in 2027, but inflation of 467.9% at the end of 2026: prices keep soaring [3][4].

Refusing the dollar is a political choice as much as an economic one: it keeps a national currency, but it will have to be made credible. According to the Rio Times, acting President Delcy Rodríguez has led the country since US forces captured Nicolás Maduro in January 2026 [3].
Venezuela has very large oil reserves. The more it produces, the more world supply can grow, which weighs on pump prices, but the road is still long.

news.2026-10-16-costa-rica-megaprison.ti: Costa Rica planned to open a 5,100-place mega-prison modelled on El Salvador's
news.2026-10-16-costa-rica-megaprison.su: The high-security centre against organised crime was due to open on 14 October. It is inspired by Nayib Bukele's giant prison in El Salvador.
news.2026-10-16-costa-rica-megaprison.po: Costa Rica announced that its Centre for High Containment of Organised Crime (CACCO) would open on Wednesday 14 October at 12:30, in the La Reforma prison complex [1]. We did not find a report of the ceremony itself.
The prison can hold 5,100 inmates and is inspired by CECOT, the Salvadoran mega-prison; El Salvador provided the plans. Its cost is around 35 million dollars [2][3].

Costa Rican media said Nayib Bukele and the Colombian president would attend, without confirmation from the presidency. Human rights organisations denounce abuses at CECOT, which the Salvadoran government denies [1][2].
news.2026-10-16-costa-rica-megaprison.wh: Costa Rica, long known for its calm, is copying a hard-line method from its neighbour in the face of rising organised crime. The new president, Laura Fernández, embraces this model [4].
The project is meant to raise the country's prison capacity by 40% [3]. Whether this choice will really reduce violence remains to be seen.
news.2026-10-16-costa-rica-megaprison.fo: You may see this model cited in other countries: security is becoming a central issue in elections across Latin America.

news.2026-10-16-grece-un-milliard-energi: Brussels allows Greece to spend one billion euros on energy outside the spending cap
The European Union agreed to extend Greece's “escape clause” to energy: batteries, heat pumps and trains paid for by the country itself.
On 9 October, the European Union agreed, for Greece only, to extend the existing national escape clause to energy resilience spending [1][2].
Greece plans about one billion euros of investment: energy storage, household equipment, public buildings and transport. It finances them with its own resources, not a new EU grant [1][2].
Projects include 200 million euros for batteries linked to renewables, 200 million for heat pumps and solar water heaters, and 320 million for rail safety and expansion [2].
Normally, a European country must limit the growth of its spending. Here, Greece can exceed that limit by up to 0.3% of GDP a year, and 0.6% in total until 2028, for this energy spending [1][2].
Note: these sums still count towards the deficit and the debt [1][2]. The exception also makes energy a matter of sovereignty: European states want better protection when prices soar.
If you pay energy bills, this is the kind of decision that, in time, can help stabilise them. For now, it is a signal that Brussels is relaxing its rules for energy.

news.2026-10-16-irak-syrie-petrole-conto: To bypass Hormuz, Iraq turns to Syria: petrol by truck, a pipeline under study
A Syrian terminal receives petrol bound for Iraq, and an Iraqi pipeline crossing Syria is being studied.

Syria has begun moving imported petrol to Iraq through its Baniyas oil terminal under a renewable three-month agreement, according to the Syrian state news agency as reported by analysts. The border crossing between the two countries is already used for oil and gas trade [2][3].

An Iraqi pipeline network would run from Haditha to Baniyas across Syria, with an initial capacity of about two million barrels a day, which would let Iraq export without going through the Strait of Hormuz [1].
The IMF attributes the contraction of the Middle East economy in 2026 to the prolonged closure of Hormuz [4].
When a strait closes, you need another way out. Iraq, very dependent on oil, is looking for an exit through the Mediterranean, via a country that is barely emerging from civil war [1].

Nothing is built yet: analysts speak of an opportunity rather than an accomplished fact, with major security and financing difficulties [1]. Traffic figures come mostly from Syrian state media and analyses, so they should be taken with caution [2][3].
The more routes there are to move Gulf oil out, the less a blockage of Hormuz pushes up the price of petrol in France. These solutions remain partial, though.

news.2026-10-16-casca-plus-rail-asie-cen: Six Central Asian and Caucasus railways join forces to send more goods from China to Europe
Meeting in Tashkent, the railway operators of six countries signed a protocol to speed up freight on the “CASCA+” route.
On 7 and 8 October in Tashkent, the railways of Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Georgia and Türkiye signed a protocol on the CASCA+ route [1][2].
On the agenda: raising freight volumes, offering competitive tariffs for refrigerated containers, ensuring a regular supply of container wagons and reducing container waiting times in ports [1].
The “plus” in CASCA+ means other interested countries can join the route. The aim is to increase traffic from Asia, in particular China, to Europe [1][3].
Today, much of the China–Europe trade goes by sea or through Russia. These countries want to turn their railways into an alternative running through the south, via the Caspian and the Caucasus.
The sources consulted give neither a volume target nor precise tariffs: this is an agreement on method, not yet proof of results [1].
Many of the things you buy come from Asia. The more routes there are to carry them, the less a blockage on one of them weighs on delivery times and prices.
